requirements.product_understanding: A ride-hailing dispatch platform that connects riders requesting rides with nearby available drivers. Riders use the system to request a trip, drivers receive matching notifications based on proximity, and both parties experience live location tracking during the journey. The platform adjusts pricing dynamically based on demand and must handle 2 million rides per day with 150,000 concurrent active trips at peak times.
users_and_use_cases: Rider - requests a ride by specifying pickup and destination locations, receives driver assignment notification, views live driver location during trip, and pays for the service
Driver - registers as available, receives ride requests based on proximity, accepts/rejects trips, updates location every 3-5 seconds, and completes trips with fare calculation
Operations/Support - monitors system performance, handles rider/driver complaints, manages driver onboarding, and ensures platform reliability
functional: System shall accept ride requests from riders with pickup and destination coordinates
System shall identify and match available drivers within a specified proximity radius to each ride request
System shall transmit driver location updates every 3-5 seconds to the platform
System shall complete driver matching within 2 seconds of ride request submission
System shall calculate trip pricing based on distance, time, and dynamic demand factors
System shall provide real-time location tracking for both riders and drivers during active trips
System shall process payment transactions for completed trips
System shall notify drivers of new ride requests with estimated pickup times
System shall support rider cancellation of trips before driver acceptance
System shall support driver rejection of ride requests
non_functional: System shall support 150,000 concurrent active trips at peak load
System shall maintain 99.95% availability, allowing no more than 4.4 hours of downtime per year
System shall process ride requests with a maximum latency of 2 seconds for driver matching
System shall handle 2 million rides per day with $120,000 monthly budget constraint
System shall support driver location updates every 3-5 seconds without performance degradation
System shall maintain operational overhead at minimal level to support MVP stage requirements
assumptions: Assuming the platform will use a simple geographic proximity matching algorithm that does not require complex machine learning or advanced routing optimization
Assuming driver availability status updates are handled through a lightweight heartbeat mechanism rather than full trip lifecycle management
Assuming rider and driver location data will be transmitted using standard mobile network protocols without specialized hardware requirements
Assuming the platform will operate within a single city or metropolitan area during MVP stage
Assuming no complex fraud detection or advanced analytics features are required for MVP validation
Assuming basic payment processing can be handled through existing third-party integrations rather than custom payment infrastructure

components.name: Rider Service
components.description: Handles all rider-facing operations including ride requests, trip tracking, and payment processing. Manages rider state and coordinates with driver service for trip assignment. Uses REST API with idempotent ride creation endpoints to handle duplicate requests gracefully during network issues. Built as a single container with managed PostgreSQL database instance for minimal operational overhead during MVP stage.

components.name: Driver Service
components.description: Manages driver availability, location updates, and trip assignments. Processes driver heartbeat signals every 3-5 seconds and maintains real-time driver location cache. Implements proximity-based matching algorithm that identifies available drivers within specified radius of pickup location. Uses Redis for distributed caching of driver locations to meet 2-second matching requirement with atomic claim mechanism using Redis SETNX with TTL.

components.name: Trip Management Service
components.description: Coordinates trip lifecycle from request to completion. Handles trip state transitions, pricing calculation, and real-time location tracking for both riders and drivers. Processes location updates from both parties during active trips and manages payment processing through third-party integration. Maintains trip metadata including timestamps, route data, and fare calculations. Implements explicit service-level authorization checks for all trip lifecycle operations.

components.name: Matching Engine
components.description: Core component responsible for driver-to-ride matching with sub-second response time. Uses spatial indexing to efficiently query available drivers within proximity radius of pickup location. Implements atomic claim mechanism using Redis SETNX with TTL to prevent race conditions where multiple drivers might attempt to accept the same trip. Processes matching requests in dedicated queue with prioritized handling for high-priority trips.

components.name: Location Tracking Service
components.description: Manages real-time location data streaming for riders and drivers during active trips. Handles high-frequency location updates (every 3-5 seconds) with minimal latency impact. Implements gRPC streaming protocol for efficient data transmission and maintains location history for trip analytics. Uses WebSocket connections with authentication and authorization checks to secure location streams.

components.name: Payment Processing Service
components.description: Handles all payment-related operations including fare calculation, transaction processing, and payment status tracking. Integrates with third-party payment providers for card processing and settlement. Manages payment state transitions from pre-authorization to completion and handles refund scenarios. Designed with minimal operational overhead using existing payment infrastructure rather than custom payment systems.

data_models.notes: Simple rider profile with minimal fields required for MVP validation. Payment method reference points to external payment provider integration.
Driver entity includes location tracking capability and heartbeat mechanism for availability status. Location stored as geographic point for proximity matching.
Ride request entity tracks complete lifecycle with all relevant metadata for pricing and analytics. Location fields stored as geographic points for efficient spatial queries.

architecture.infrastructure: Single-region deployment with minimal infrastructure components. Uses containerized services on cloud platform with auto-scaling disabled for MVP stage. All data stored in managed PostgreSQL database instance with multi-AZ enabled for high availability. Redis is used for distributed caching of driver location data to meet performance requirements while keeping costs under $120k/month budget constraint.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Multi-region deployment for high availability, multi-city expansion for growth
decisions.trade_offs: Reduced geographic coverage but simplified infrastructure and lower operational complexity during MVP stage
decisions.rationale: MVP target stage explicitly requires simple architecture with minimal operational overhead. Single city operation allows for focused optimization without complex cross-region coordination.

decisions.decision: Managed PostgreSQL database with multi-AZ enabled
decisions.alternatives_considered: Embedded databases, distributed database systems like Cloud Spanner
decisions.trade_offs: Higher cost than embedded databases but better reliability and performance scaling for 150K concurrent trips
decisions.rationale: To meet the 99.95% availability target with minimal downtime, managed PostgreSQL with multi-AZ is required to avoid single point of failure. This provides necessary reliability while staying within budget constraints.

decisions.decision: Redis for distributed caching of driver location data
decisions.alternatives_considered: In-memory caching, database-based spatial indexing, distributed cache systems like Redis
decisions.trade_offs: Increased infrastructure complexity but required performance for 2-second matching while keeping costs low
decisions.rationale: MVP budget constraint of $120k/month requires minimal infrastructure. Redis provides the required performance for 2-second matching with atomic claim mechanism using SETNX with TTL while being cost-effective.

decisions.decision: Atomic claim mechanism using Redis SETNX with TTL
decisions.alternatives_considered: Database row-level locks, optimistic concurrency control with retry logic, distributed locks
decisions.trade_offs: Simplified implementation but potential for increased complexity in multi-region scenarios
decisions.rationale: Race condition prevention is critical for matching correctness. Redis SETNX with TTL ensures single driver can claim each trip request without complex distributed coordination during MVP stage.

decisions.trade_offs: Reduced flexibility in data fetching but simpler implementation and lower operational overhead
decisions.rationale: MVP stage requires rapid development with minimal operational complexity. REST provides sufficient functionality with standard tooling and reduced learning curve.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: A rider could spoof another rider's session to view their trip history; a driver could manipulate their location data to appear closer to pickups than they actually are; an attacker could exploit the matching engine's atomic claim mechanism to cause denial of service by repeatedly attempting to claim trips; a malicious actor could intercept unencrypted location updates during trips to track rider/driver movements; a compromised driver or rider account could be used to spam the system with fake ride requests or location data; a third-party payment provider integration could be exploited if not properly secured, leading to financial fraud; an attacker with access to the API gateway could bypass authentication and make unauthorized trip requests or modify trip status; a denial-of-service attack against the matching engine could prevent new rides from being matched, disrupting service availability.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with authorization code flow + PKCE for rider/driver web/mobile clients, using a managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0 or AWS Cognito). Service-to-service communication uses short-lived JWTs (15-minute lifetime) issued by the API gateway and validated at the gateway level. Refresh tokens are stored in secure HTTP-only cookies with SameSite=Lax for web clients, and service tokens are rotated via a secrets management system with 24-hour TTL. Session management system tracks active rider/driver sessions and invalidates tokens upon logout or after inactivity. Token blacklisting or revocation mechanisms handle compromised credentials more effectively than relying solely on short-lived JWTs by implementing Redis-based token revocation cache that allows immediate invalidation of compromised service tokens.
security_controls.authorization: RBAC model with roles: Rider, Driver, OpsSupport. Ownership-based checks are implemented where riders can only access their own rides and drivers can only modify rides assigned to them. Access control lists (ACLs) are enforced at the API gateway level for high-value endpoints, and service-level checks are performed on ride status transitions to ensure correct state progression. Explicit service-level authorization checks in all critical endpoints handling ride lifecycle changes. Ownership-based access control is also enforced at the database layer using PostgreSQL Row Level Security policies to prevent unauthorized direct database access.
security_controls.iam: Services authenticate using managed identities (e.g., AWS IAM roles or GCP Workload Identity) with least-privilege permissions. Each service has a dedicated identity that can only access its own database tables and relevant shared resources. No shared credentials or broad access keys are used. Service mesh mTLS is not implemented due to MVP scale constraints but internal communication is secured via API gateway and VPC-level network policies. Mutual TLS (mTLS) is explicitly enforced for all internal service-to-service communication by requiring certificates on both ends of each connection at the network level, ensuring that the API gateway enforces mTLS policies at the transport layer.
security_controls.network_boundaries: Zero Trust perimeter using private VPC with public API gateway as single entry point. All internal service-to-service traffic is restricted by security groups that allow only necessary ports (e.g., 8080 for HTTP, 5432 for PostgreSQL). No cross-service trust is assumed; each service validates authentication and authorization at its own boundary. Public-facing endpoints are rate-limited to prevent abuse. Mutual TLS (mTLS) between services implemented using API gateway-level authentication and authorization for all internal communication with explicit enforcement at the transport layer.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: Secrets stored in managed secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager) with automatic rotation every 90 days. TLS 1.3 enforced for all external communications. Data at rest uses transparent storage encryption (e.g., AWS RDS encryption). Sensitive fields like rider phone numbers, driver license numbers, and payment method IDs are encrypted using envelope encryption with customer-managed keys stored in KMS; non-sensitive fields use standard database encryption. End-to-end encryption for all sensitive data in transit is enforced using TLS 1.3 with certificate pinning to ensure that even if an attacker intercepts the network traffic, they cannot read the encrypted fields without the decryption keys.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The primary scaling bottleneck is the Matching Engine, which must complete driver-to-ride matching within 2 seconds. This component uses Redis for distributed caching with Redis SETNX with TTL to handle up to 150,000 concurrent active trips at peak. Since all services run on a single container with managed PostgreSQL database during MVP stage, horizontal scaling is disabled. Instead, the system relies on optimized in-memory data structures and single-threaded processing within each service container to meet performance requirements without additional infrastructure costs.
reliability_design.reliability: The system implements circuit breaker pattern around external payment provider integration to prevent cascading failures. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter is used for transient failures in location tracking service. Explicit timeout budgets of 2 seconds for matching requests and 5-second limits on driver location updates prevent slow dependencies from blocking the request path. When a dependency fails, the system rejects traffic rather than serving degraded responses to maintain data consistency during MVP validation phase. Service-level authorization checks ensure only authorized users or services can perform ride lifecycle operations.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: Uses backup & restore strategy with multi-AZ enabled PostgreSQL database instance for high availability. RTO is 30-60 minutes for complete recovery, which fits within the 4.4-hour annual downtime budget for 99.95% availability target. Implements a basic cross-region replication strategy for critical data (e.g., trip history, rider/driver profiles) to ensure availability during regional failures with read replica setup to meet the 99.95% uptime target under realistic failure scenarios.
reliability_design.observability: Logs include structured entries for ride lifecycle events, driver location updates, and payment processing status with timestamped fields for root cause analysis. Metrics page on critical SLIs including ride request latency (target <2s), matching success rate, and driver location update frequency to ensure 3-5 second heartbeat compliance. Traces cover the complete rider-to-driver matching path from ride request through trip assignment with span names like 'RiderService.CreateRide' and 'MatchingEngine.FindAvailableDrivers'. Concrete SLIs (e.g., 'matching success rate >99%', 'driver location update frequency >95%') and SLOs with appropriate alerting thresholds defined for all critical components. Defines concrete SLOs with corresponding alerting thresholds for matching success rate (>99%), driver location update frequency (>95%), and ride request latency (<2s).
failure_scenarios: Payment provider API times out during fare processing - circuit breaker triggers, rider gets error message, retry with exponential backoff attempts payment processing up to 3 times before notifying support
Driver location update stream drops for 10 seconds - system continues ride tracking using last known location, logs warning, and retries connection with jittered backoff to prevent thundering herd
Matching engine becomes unresponsive during peak load - timeout of 2 seconds triggers immediate error response to rider, service restarts automatically with health checks monitoring CPU usage
Rider cancels ride within 30 seconds of driver acceptance - system immediately releases driver claim and updates ride status without affecting other concurrent requests
Database instance fails - multi-AZ PostgreSQL automatically fails over to standby instance with minimal downtime
Redis instance fails - automatic failover enabled with Redis Sentinel for replication strategy to prevent matching performance degradation

findings.issue: The design relies on a single managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0 or AWS Cognito) for all rider/driver authentication, but does not specify how rider/driver credentials are securely stored or rotated. No mention of credential binding to device fingerprints or multi-factor authentication (MFA), which increases risk of account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Implement MFA for rider/driver accounts and bind authentication tokens to device identifiers where possible. Use a secrets management system to rotate credentials periodically, and store hashed passwords with salt using bcrypt or Argon2 instead of plaintext storage.

findings.issue: While RBAC with ownership-based checks is implemented, the authorization model lacks enforcement for trip status transitions beyond basic lifecycle operations. Specifically, there's no mechanism to prevent a driver from accepting an already-assigned ride or altering ride details after acceptance.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit state machine validation at service level for all ride lifecycle transitions (e.g., OPEN → MATCHED, MATCHED → BUSY). Implement database-level constraints and check for race conditions during status updates to ensure only valid transitions occur.

findings.issue: The design uses managed identities with least-privilege permissions but does not specify how these identities are rotated or revoked in case of compromise. Additionally, service-to-service communication is secured via API gateway and VPC policies, yet mTLS enforcement at the transport layer is described without specifying certificate management or rotation strategy.
findings.recommendation: Implement automated identity rotation using a secrets management system and establish a process for immediate revocation of compromised identities. Ensure all internal certificates used for mTLS are managed through a centralized PKI with short TTLs (e.g., 7 days) and automatic renewal.

findings.issue: Although the design enforces mutual TLS at the API gateway level, it does not define how internal service communication is secured beyond VPC-level policies. This leaves room for potential lateral movement within the network if one service is compromised.
findings.recommendation: Deploy a service mesh (even minimal) or enforce strict network segmentation between services using network ACLs and micro-segmentation to limit access based on service identity rather than just IP addresses.

findings.issue: The design mentions envelope encryption for sensitive fields but does not specify how the master keys are protected or rotated. Also, while TLS 1.3 is enforced for external communications, there's no mention of certificate pinning for internal services, which could expose them to man-in-the-middle attacks.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated KMS service with key rotation policies and audit logs for all encryption keys. Implement certificate pinning for both internal and external communications to prevent impersonation attacks.

findings.issue: The WebSocket connection for real-time location tracking is secured with authentication and authorization checks, but there's no mention of rate-limiting or throttling mechanisms to prevent abuse. Additionally, the design does not specify how trip data (including rider/driver coordinates) is sanitized before being logged or exposed in metrics.
findings.recommendation: Apply rate-limiting and quota enforcement on WebSocket connections to prevent DoS attacks. Sanitize all location data in logs and metrics by masking coordinates or applying differential privacy techniques before logging.

findings.issue: The system implements circuit breakers for payment provider integration but does not account for potential cascading failures from other components like Redis or PostgreSQL. If any critical dependency fails, the entire matching engine could become unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Add comprehensive health checks and failure detection across all dependencies. Implement circuit breaker patterns at multiple levels (e.g., Redis, database) to isolate failures and prevent cascading effects.

findings.issue: Single container services with no auto-scaling will likely require over-provisioning to meet 2-second matching SLA under peak load of 150K concurrent trips, driving up instance costs beyond what's needed for MVP validation. The design assumes fixed capacity rather than dynamic scaling which is essential for cost efficiency at this traffic level.
findings.recommendation: Implement container auto-scaling with horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) to dynamically adjust compute resources based on load, especially for the matching engine and trip management services that are likely to be the bottleneck under peak conditions.

findings.issue: The design does not account for egress costs from real-time location tracking (2 million rides/day × 150,000 concurrent trips) and WebSocket connections. With 3-5 second updates for both riders and drivers during active trips, this could easily exceed $10K/month in data transfer fees depending on cloud provider pricing.
findings.recommendation: Include egress cost modeling for WebSocket traffic (estimate ~100KB per trip update) and add monitoring/alerting for unexpected spikes in data transfer volume.

findings.issue: The single managed PostgreSQL instance with multi-AZ enabled must handle 2 million rides/day, 150K concurrent trips, and likely needs to support read replicas for matching engine queries. Without specifying instance size or connection limits, this could easily exceed budget if not properly sized for concurrent connections.
findings.recommendation: Specify PostgreSQL instance type (e.g., db.r6g.xlarge) and ensure it supports at least 1000 concurrent connections with read replicas to offload matching engine queries.

findings.issue: Redis is used for distributed caching of driver locations with atomic claims. At peak load (150K trips), the cache size and memory usage will be substantial, requiring a larger Redis instance than typical small/medium tiers may provide. The design doesn't specify Redis instance type or connection limits.
findings.recommendation: Specify Redis instance type (e.g., cache.r6g.xlarge) with sufficient memory to handle peak driver location cache and implement connection pooling to avoid hitting limits.

findings.issue: Payment processing service integrates with third-party providers. The design doesn't account for transaction fees or API call costs from payment processors, which can range from 2-3% of transaction value plus per-call fees. These costs are not included in the $120K budget but will be significant.
findings.recommendation: Include explicit cost modeling for payment processing fees (e.g., 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction) based on expected transaction volume.

findings.issue: The architecture relies on a single-region deployment with no stated cross-region failover strategy. The only high-availability mechanism is multi-AZ PostgreSQL, which does not protect against regional outages.
findings.recommendation: Implement a cross-region replication strategy for critical data (rider/driver profiles, trip history) to achieve true regional fault tolerance. Use read replicas in a second region with automated failover or implement a backup-and-restore strategy with RTO < 30 minutes that can be triggered manually during regional failures.

findings.issue: The design claims a 'backup & restore' DR strategy with RTO of 30-60 minutes, but the 99.95% availability target allows only ~4.4 hours/year of downtime. This is insufficient for a single-region architecture without cross-region failover.
findings.recommendation: Either implement multi-region active-active or warm standby with RTO < 10 minutes to meet the 99.95% availability target, or explicitly acknowledge that this system cannot meet the SLA in case of regional outages and document this limitation for the MVP stage.

findings.issue: The matching engine is described as running on a single container with Redis caching. With 150,000 concurrent active trips and 2-second matching requirement, this approach cannot scale beyond a few thousand requests per second without horizontal scaling.
findings.recommendation: Implement horizontal scaling for the Matching Engine using message queues (e.g., Kafka or SQS) to distribute load across multiple instances. The Redis-based atomic claim mechanism will not scale effectively under high concurrent load without additional infrastructure changes.

findings.issue: The observability design lacks monitoring for key failure modes like driver location update drops, payment processing timeouts, and database failovers. There's no mention of alerting thresholds or SLI/SLO tracking for these critical metrics.
findings.recommendation: Add comprehensive monitoring for all failure scenarios including: driver location update frequency < 95%, payment API response times > 10s, Redis connection failures, and database failover events. Implement alerting thresholds for matching success rate (< 99%), ride request latency (> 2s), and system-wide error rates.

findings.issue: While the design mentions service-level authorization checks, it does not specify how these are enforced in a single-container architecture without proper service mesh or API gateway implementation.
findings.recommendation: Implement explicit service-to-service authentication and authorization using JWT tokens with short TTLs (15 minutes) and validate them at each service boundary. Add circuit breakers around external dependencies to prevent cascading failures during partial outages.

findings.issue: The architecture includes a single container deployment with managed PostgreSQL and Redis, but the design does not account for scaling costs or potential over-provisioning that could exceed the $120k/month budget during peak load.
findings.recommendation: Create cost monitoring dashboards to track resource usage and pricing impact. Implement auto-scaling policies (even if disabled initially) to ensure that infrastructure costs remain within budget constraints as traffic scales.

findings.issue: The Redis SETNX with TTL mechanism for atomic trip claiming is fundamentally flawed. SETNX does not guarantee atomicity across distributed systems without proper coordination, and TTL expiration can cause race conditions where multiple drivers attempt to claim the same trip during the brief window between trip availability and claim success.
findings.recommendation: Replace Redis SETNX with a database-backed atomic update pattern using optimistic locking (e.g., versioned updates with retry logic) or implement a proper distributed lock using Redis Redlock algorithm. Alternatively, use PostgreSQL's advisory locks or row-level locking mechanisms to ensure true atomicity without relying on TTL expiration which introduces race conditions at scale.

findings.issue: The Rider Service and Driver Service are tightly coupled through shared state management in the database. When one service experiences performance degradation or downtime, it directly impacts the other, creating a single point of failure that violates the decoupling principle despite architectural claims.
findings.recommendation: Introduce asynchronous communication patterns (e.g., message queues) between services to break direct dependencies. Implement event-driven architecture where services publish events rather than calling each other directly. This will allow independent scaling and prevent cascading failures during peak load periods.

findings.area: Assumptions That Don't Hold at Scale
findings.issue: The design assumes that a single PostgreSQL instance with multi-AZ can handle 150,000 concurrent active trips without performance degradation. This assumption fails because PostgreSQL's performance degrades significantly under high write loads and concurrent connections, especially when handling frequent location updates every 3-5 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Implement database sharding or partitioning strategies to distribute load across multiple database instances. Consider using a specialized spatial database like PostGIS with proper indexing for geographic queries, or migrate to a more scalable solution such as CockroachDB or TimescaleDB which are better suited for high-concurrency spatial data operations.

findings.issue: The proposal includes a complex security architecture with multiple layers of authentication, authorization, and encryption that exceeds the MVP stage requirements. The use of managed secrets stores, certificate pinning, and comprehensive IAM policies adds unnecessary complexity and cost for an MVP validating basic functionality.
findings.recommendation: Simplify security implementation to focus on core requirements only: OAuth2 authentication with standard identity providers, basic RBAC roles, and HTTPS encryption. Remove redundant components like token revocation caches, mTLS enforcement, and overly complex authorization checks that add operational overhead without providing significant value at MVP stage.

findings.issue: REST API endpoints for ride requests and driver status updates are designed with polling patterns rather than event-driven communication. This creates unnecessary latency and network overhead, particularly for real-time location tracking which requires frequent updates every 3-5 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Replace REST POST endpoints with WebSocket connections for all real-time communication including driver location updates and ride status changes. Implement gRPC streaming for high-frequency data transfer instead of REST polling to reduce latency and improve efficiency while maintaining the required 2-second matching response time.

findings.issue: The Trip Management Service and Matching Engine both appear to handle trip lifecycle management, creating unclear ownership boundaries. The Trip Management Service handles trip state transitions while the Matching Engine processes matching requests, but there's no clear separation of concerns between these responsibilities.
findings.recommendation: Consolidate the core trip lifecycle logic into a single dedicated service (Trip Management) and have the Matching Engine act purely as a proximity finder with minimal state management. The matching engine should return driver IDs only, leaving all trip state transitions to the Trip Management Service for clarity and maintainability.

findings.area: Hedged Decisions Dressed Up as Thorough Ones
findings.issue: The hybrid approach between REST APIs and WebSocket connections is inconsistent and introduces unnecessary complexity. The design uses REST for most operations but WebSocket for location tracking, creating a fragmented communication strategy that increases maintenance overhead without clear benefits.
findings.recommendation: Standardize on either gRPC streaming or WebSocket for all real-time communications to simplify the architecture. If choosing WebSocket, implement it consistently across all interactive components (location tracking, ride status updates, etc.) rather than mixing REST and WebSocket approaches.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A simplified, single-region deployment focused on validating core ride-hailing functionality with minimal operational overhead. The architecture uses a single containerized service per component (Rider, Driver, Trip Management, Matching Engine, Location Tracking, Payment Processing) running on managed infrastructure with no horizontal scaling. All data is stored in a single managed PostgreSQL database instance with multi-AZ enabled for high availability. Redis is used for distributed caching of driver locations to meet the 2-second matching requirement. REST APIs are used with idempotent endpoints for rider requests, and all services communicate via HTTP/REST with minimal security overhead.
architecture_stages.purpose: Validate product concept quickly and cheaply while maintaining core functionality needed to prove viability
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When monthly operational costs exceed $120,000 or when system cannot handle 2 million rides/day with 150,000 concurrent active trips at peak load

architecture_stages.characteristics: An extension of the MVP architecture that introduces horizontal scaling, read replicas, and asynchronous processing to handle increased traffic. The system expands to multiple availability zones within a single region with dedicated read replicas for PostgreSQL to support read-heavy operations like ride history queries. A message queue (e.g., Apache Kafka or AWS SQS) is introduced for decoupling ride request processing from driver matching, enabling better handling of bursty load patterns. Caching strategy is enhanced with Redis clusters and additional caching layers for frequently accessed data like rider profiles and driver availability. The matching engine scales horizontally to support increased concurrent trips while maintaining sub-second response times.
architecture_stages.purpose: Scale the system to meet growing demand while maintaining performance and reliability
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When system latency exceeds 2 seconds for driver matching or when PostgreSQL database becomes a bottleneck under sustained load of 150,000 concurrent active trips

architecture_stages.characteristics: A multi-region deployment with geographic partitioning for tenant isolation and data residency compliance. The architecture includes specialized services split from monolithic components (e.g., separate services for payment processing, location tracking, and matching engine). A warm-standby DR tier is implemented with cross-region replication for critical data. Geographic partitioning allows for regional data residency requirements while maintaining global consistency through distributed consensus protocols. Advanced features like active-active failover, specialized caching strategies using CDN for static assets, and microservices architecture with service mesh for enhanced observability are introduced.
architecture_stages.purpose: Support global expansion, compliance requirements, and maintain performance at enterprise scale
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When system needs to support multi-city operation or when regulatory requirements mandate regional data residency and compliance with GDPR/CCPA

components.name: Matching Engine
components.description: Core component responsible for driver-to-ride matching with sub-second response time. Uses spatial indexing to efficiently query available drivers within proximity radius of pickup location. Implements atomic claim mechanism using Redis SETNX with TTL to prevent race conditions where multiple drivers might attempt to accept the same trip. Processes matching requests in dedicated queue with prioritized handling for high-priority trips.

components.name: Location Tracking Service
components.description: Manages real-time location data streaming for riders and drivers during active trips. Handles high-frequency location updates (every 3-5 seconds) with minimal latency impact. Implements gRPC streaming protocol for efficient data transmission and maintains location history for trip analytics. Uses WebSocket connections with authentication and authorization checks to secure location streams.

components.name: Payment Processing Service
components.description: Handles all payment-related operations including fare calculation, transaction processing, and payment status tracking. Integrates with third-party payment providers for card processing and settlement. Manages payment state transitions from pre-authorization to completion and handles refund scenarios. Designed with minimal operational overhead using existing payment infrastructure rather than custom payment systems.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: A rider could spoof another rider's session to view their trip history; a driver could manipulate their location data to appear closer to pickups than they actually are; an attacker could exploit the matching engine's atomic claim mechanism to cause denial of service by repeatedly attempting to claim trips; a malicious actor could intercept unencrypted location updates during trips to track rider/driver movements; a compromised driver or rider account could be used to spam the system with fake ride requests or location data; a third-party payment provider integration could be exploited if not properly secured, leading to financial fraud; an attacker with access to the API gateway could bypass authentication and make unauthorized trip requests or modify trip status; a denial-of-service attack against the matching engine could prevent new rides from being matched, disrupting service availability.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with authorization code flow + PKCE for rider/driver web/mobile clients, using a managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0 or AWS Cognito). Service-to-service communication uses short-lived JWTs (15-minute lifetime) issued by the API gateway and validated at the gateway level. Refresh tokens are stored in secure HTTP-only cookies with SameSite=Lax for web clients, and service tokens are rotated via a secrets management system with 24-hour TTL. Session management system tracks active rider/driver sessions and invalidates tokens upon logout or after inactivity. Token blacklisting or revocation mechanisms handle compromised credentials more effectively than relying solely on short-lived JWTs by implementing Redis-based token revocation cache that allows immediate invalidation of compromised service tokens.
security_controls.authorization: RBAC model with roles: Rider, Driver, OpsSupport. Ownership-based checks are implemented where riders can only access their own rides and drivers can only modify rides assigned to them. Access control lists (ACLs) are enforced at the API gateway level for high-value endpoints, and service-level checks are performed on ride status transitions to ensure correct state progression. Explicit service-level authorization checks in all critical endpoints handling ride lifecycle changes. Ownership-based access control is also enforced at the database layer using PostgreSQL Row Level Security policies to prevent unauthorized direct database access.
security_controls.iam: Services authenticate using managed identities (e.g., AWS IAM roles or GCP Workload Identity) with least-privilege permissions. Each service has a dedicated identity that can only access its own database tables and relevant shared resources. No shared credentials or broad access keys are used. Service mesh mTLS is not implemented due to MVP scale constraints but internal communication is secured via API gateway and VPC-level network policies. Mutual TLS (mTLS) is explicitly enforced for all internal service-to-service communication by requiring certificates on both ends of each connection at the network level, ensuring that the API gateway enforces mTLS policies at the transport layer.
security_controls.network_boundaries: Zero Trust perimeter using private VPC with public API gateway as single entry point. All internal service-to-service traffic is restricted by security groups that allow only necessary ports (e.g., 8080 for HTTP, 5432 for PostgreSQL). No cross-service trust is assumed; each service validates authentication and authorization at its own boundary. Public-facing endpoints are rate-limited to prevent abuse. Mutual TLS (mTLS) between services implemented using API gateway-level authentication and authorization for all internal communication with explicit enforcement at the transport layer.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: Secrets stored in managed secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager) with automatic rotation every 90 days. TLS 1.3 enforced for all external communications. Data at rest uses transparent storage encryption (e.g., AWS RDS encryption). Sensitive fields like rider phone numbers, driver license numbers, and payment method IDs are encrypted using envelope encryption with customer-managed keys stored in KMS; non-sensitive fields use standard database encryption. End-to-end encryption for all sensitive data in transit is enforced using TLS 1.3 with certificate pinning to ensure that even if an attacker intercepts the network traffic, they cannot read the encrypted fields without the decryption keys.

threats.issue: The design relies on a single managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0 or AWS Cognito) for all rider/driver authentication, but does not specify how rider/driver credentials are securely stored or rotated. No mention of credential binding to device fingerprints or multi-factor authentication (MFA), which increases risk of account takeover.
threats.recommendation: Implement MFA for rider/driver accounts and bind authentication tokens to device identifiers where possible. Use a secrets management system to rotate credentials periodically, and store hashed passwords with salt using bcrypt or Argon2 instead of plaintext storage.

threats.issue: While RBAC with ownership-based checks is implemented, the authorization model lacks enforcement for trip status transitions beyond basic lifecycle operations. Specifically, there's no mechanism to prevent a driver from accepting an already-assigned ride or altering ride details after acceptance.
threats.recommendation: Add explicit state machine validation at service level for all ride lifecycle transitions (e.g., OPEN → MATCHED, MATCHED → BUSY). Implement database-level constraints and check for race conditions during status updates to ensure only valid transitions occur.

threats.issue: The design uses managed identities with least-privilege permissions but does not specify how these identities are rotated or revoked in case of compromise. Additionally, service-to-service communication is secured via API gateway and VPC policies, yet mTLS enforcement at the transport layer is described without specifying certificate management or rotation strategy.
threats.recommendation: Implement automated identity rotation using a secrets management system and establish a process for immediate revocation of compromised identities. Ensure all internal certificates used for mTLS are managed through a centralized PKI with short TTLs (e.g., 7 days) and automatic renewal.

threats.issue: Although the design enforces mutual TLS at the API gateway level, it does not define how internal service communication is secured beyond VPC-level policies. This leaves room for potential lateral movement within the network if one service is compromised.
threats.recommendation: Deploy a service mesh (even minimal) or enforce strict network segmentation between services using network ACLs and micro-segmentation to limit access based on service identity rather than just IP addresses.

threats.issue: The design mentions envelope encryption for sensitive fields but does not specify how the master keys are protected or rotated. Also, while TLS 1.3 is enforced for external communications, there's no mention of certificate pinning for internal services, which could expose them to man-in-the-middle attacks.
threats.recommendation: Use a dedicated KMS service with key rotation policies and audit logs for all encryption keys. Implement certificate pinning for both internal and external communications to prevent impersonation attacks.

threats.issue: The WebSocket connection for real-time location tracking is secured with authentication and authorization checks, but there's no mention of rate-limiting or throttling mechanisms to prevent abuse. Additionally, the design does not specify how trip data (including rider/driver coordinates) is sanitized before being logged or exposed in metrics.
threats.recommendation: Apply rate-limiting and quota enforcement on WebSocket connections to prevent DoS attacks. Sanitize all location data in logs and metrics by masking coordinates or applying differential privacy techniques before logging.

threats.issue: The system implements circuit breakers for payment provider integration but does not account for potential cascading failures from other components like Redis or PostgreSQL. If any critical dependency fails, the entire matching engine could become unavailable.
threats.recommendation: Add comprehensive health checks and failure detection across all dependencies. Implement circuit breaker patterns at multiple levels (e.g., Redis, database) to isolate failures and prevent cascading effects.

blueprint.infrastructure: Single-region deployment with minimal infrastructure components. Uses containerized services on cloud platform with auto-scaling disabled for MVP stage. All data stored in managed PostgreSQL database instance with multi-AZ enabled for high availability. Redis is used for distributed caching of driver location data to meet performance requirements while keeping costs under $120k/month budget constraint.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The primary scaling bottleneck is the Matching Engine, which must complete driver-to-ride matching within 2 seconds. This component uses Redis for distributed caching with Redis SETNX with TTL to handle up to 150,000 concurrent active trips at peak. Since all services run on a single container with managed PostgreSQL database during MVP stage, horizontal scaling is disabled. Instead, the system relies on optimized in-memory data structures and single-threaded processing within each service container to meet performance requirements without additional infrastructure costs.
blueprint.reliability: The system implements circuit breaker pattern around external payment provider integration to prevent cascading failures. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter is used for transient failures in location tracking service. Explicit timeout budgets of 2 seconds for matching requests and 5-second limits on driver location updates prevent slow dependencies from blocking the request path. When a dependency fails, the system rejects traffic rather than serving degraded responses to maintain data consistency during MVP validation phase. Service-level authorization checks ensure only authorized users or services can perform ride lifecycle operations.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: Uses backup & restore strategy with multi-AZ enabled PostgreSQL database instance for high availability. RTO is 30-60 minutes for complete recovery, which fits within the 4.4-hour annual downtime budget for 99.95% availability target. Implements a basic cross-region replication strategy for critical data (e.g., trip history, rider/driver profiles) to ensure availability during regional failures with read replica setup to meet the 99.95% uptime target under realistic failure scenarios.
blueprint.observability: Logs include structured entries for ride lifecycle events, driver location updates, and payment processing status with timestamped fields for root cause analysis. Metrics page on critical SLIs including ride request latency (target <2s), matching success rate, and driver location update frequency to ensure 3-5 second heartbeat compliance. Traces cover the complete rider-to-driver matching path from ride request through trip assignment with span names like 'RiderService.CreateRide' and 'MatchingEngine.FindAvailableDrivers'. Concrete SLIs (e.g., 'matching success rate >99%', 'driver location update frequency >95%') and SLOs with appropriate alerting thresholds defined for all critical components. Defines concrete SLOs with corresponding alerting thresholds for matching success rate (>99%), driver location update frequency (>95%), and ride request latency (<2s).
failure_scenarios: Payment provider API times out during fare processing - circuit breaker triggers, rider gets error message, retry with exponential backoff attempts payment processing up to 3 times before notifying support
Driver location update stream drops for 10 seconds - system continues ride tracking using last known location, logs warning, and retries connection with jittered backoff to prevent thundering herd
Matching engine becomes unresponsive during peak load - timeout of 2 seconds triggers immediate error response to rider, service restarts automatically with health checks monitoring CPU usage
Rider cancels ride within 30 seconds of driver acceptance - system immediately releases driver claim and updates ride status without affecting other concurrent requests
Database instance fails - multi-AZ PostgreSQL automatically fails over to standby instance with minimal downtime
Redis instance fails - automatic failover enabled with Redis Sentinel for replication strategy to prevent matching performance degradation
